title: Early-life inhalant allergen exposure, filaggrin genotype, and the development of sensitization from infancy to adolescence.
ehr_evidence: The Manchester Asthma and Allergy Study is an unselected birth cohort; dust samples were collected in the first year of life, sensitization was assessed by skin prick tests at 6 time points, FLG genotyping was performed, and cat/dog ownership was ascertained by questionnaires administered at home visits.
summary: In a population-based birth cohort followed from infancy to age 16 years, early-life inhalant allergen exposure (mite, cat, dog) interacted with FLG loss-of-function mutations to modify the development of allergic sensitization.
key_findings: Significant interaction between FLG and Fel d 1 exposure on cat sensitization from infancy to age 16 years (OR 1.36; 95% CI 1.02-1.80; P = .035), with greater effect among children with FLG mutations.
Interaction between FLG and Der p 1 (mite) exposure did not reach statistical significance in multivariable models.

Significant interaction between FLG genotype and dog ownership on sensitization to any allergen, with markedly lower risk among children with FLG mutations who had a dog in infancy (OR 0.16; 95% CI 0.03-0.86; P = .03).
Children with FLG mutations and a cat at home had the greatest probability of cat sensitization during childhood (OR 3.02; 95% CI 1.26-7.21; P = .013).
captured_features: Dust allergen concentrations (Der p 1, Fel d 1, Can f 1)
Cat and dog ownership in first year of life
Allergen-specific sensitization by skin prick test
pathologies_diseases: Allergic sensitization (cat, house dust mite, dog)
study_design: Cohort (population-based birth cohort with longitudinal follow-up)
population: Children from the Manchester Asthma and Allergy Study birth cohort, followed from infancy to age 16 years (white participants with complete FLG genotyping and dust samples)
exposure_domain: Indoor/inhalant allergens (house dust mite, cat, dog allergen exposure and pet ownership)
limitations: Reduced sample size due to incomplete FLG genotyping and limited early-life dust sample availability.
All participants were white, so results are not applicable to other ethnicities.
Smaller sample size at age 1 year and in some subgroups.
Could not address relative importance of infancy versus later-childhood exposure.
